🧰 Use AI well · Step 1 of 4 · 5 min

Ask so that AI understands

The four parts of a good request, and what to do with a weak answer.

💬 A chatbot cannot read your mind

A chatbot is a program that answers your messages. It has learned a lot about the world from a huge amount of text, but it does not know you. It cannot see your homework, and it does not know how old you are or what you already know.

It has only your words, so everything it needs must be in your message. A message to a chatbot is called a prompt: it is your request, the thing you ask it to do.

Most chatbots have a minimum age. Often it is 13, and under 18 you may need a parent's permission. If you are under the minimum age, use a chatbot only together with an adult.

Task. You need help with a school talk about volcanoes. Which request is most likely to get a useful answer?

Show the answer

Right answer: “I am 12. I am giving a 3-minute talk on volcanoes to my class. Give me 5 surprising facts in simple words.”

The best request says who is asking and why, what to do and how the answer should look. The long polite one has many words, but it still does not say exactly what is needed. Being polite is fine, but it is not enough.

🧱 Four parts of a good request

You can build a good request from four parts. Not every request needs all four. But when an answer disappoints you, one of them is often missing.

Here is one request, split into its parts:

Context (who you are and why you need the answer): “I am 10. I am making a birthday card for my grandmother, who loves her garden.”
Task (what the chatbot should do): “Write a poem for her.”
Format (how the answer should look: its length, a list, a table): “Four lines that rhyme.”
Limits (what the chatbot should avoid): “Do not mention her age.”

Your age or what you already know is enough to say who you are. Never type your full name, your address or a password into a chatbot.

Task. Here is one request, line by line. Which part of a request is each line?

Show the solution

Who is asking and why: context. What to do: task. How the answer should look: format. What to avoid: limits.

Task. Is the request clear, or too vague? A vague request makes the chatbot guess what you want.

Show the solution

A clear request says exactly what to do, and often how long the answer should be and who it is for. A vague one leaves questions unanswered. Which homework? Interesting for whom? Better in what way?

🔁 The first answer is a draft

Think of a chatbot's first answer as a draft: a first try that can be improved. If it is not what you need, write back: “shorter”, “give an example”, “I did not understand step 2: explain it another way”.

Inside one chat (one conversation) the chatbot can see the earlier messages, so you do not have to start again. A new chat usually starts from zero.

You: What is a fraction?
Chatbot: A fraction is a ratio of two whole numbers: a numerator and a denominator …
You: I did not understand “ratio”. I am 9: explain it with a pizza.

Task. A chatbot's explanation is too hard for you. What is the best thing to do next?

Show the answer

Right answer: Say which part you did not understand and ask for a simpler explanation with an example

When you say what was hard, the chatbot can explain exactly that part in a new way. The same question, in this chat or in a new one, may get a different answer, but the chatbot still does not know what you did not understand.

🎯 Two more tricks

Show an example of what you want: “Here is a riddle I like: What has hands but cannot clap? A clock. Write 3 more like it.” The chatbot usually notices the pattern and follows it.

Let it ask you first: “Before you answer, ask me 3 questions about what I need.” Its questions often show what was missing from your request.

Task. Look at this request: “I am 12 and I am preparing a talk for my class. Explain what a black hole is. Do not use formulas.” Which part of a good request is missing?

Show the answer

Right answer: The format: how the answer should look

The four parts are context, task, format and limits. This request has context (12, a talk for the class), a task (explain) and a limit (no formulas). It does not say how long the answer should be or what form it should take.

Think first. Why can the same question get a different answer each time?

Show the answer

A chatbot does not keep ready-made answers. It writes a new one each time, word by word, and its choice of words is a little random.

That helps when you want ideas, such as a name or the first line of a story: ask again, or ask for three versions and choose the best one.

It also means that two answers can disagree. So an answer is not automatically a fact: the next step of your path is about that.

Task. You want a chatbot to write quiz questions in exactly the style your teacher uses. What is the best thing to do?

Show the answer

Right answer: Give it one of your teacher's questions as an example

The chatbot does not know your teacher, so “in my teacher's style” tells it nothing. One real example shows the style, and the chatbot can follow the pattern. Capital letters and new chats add no information.

Remember

  • A chatbot cannot read your mind. Put everything it needs into your request (your prompt).
  • Build a request from four parts: context, task, format and limits. When an answer disappoints you, look for the missing one.
  • The first answer is a draft. Write back and say exactly what to change.
  • Show an example of what you want, or let the chatbot ask you questions first.
